label: t.slices
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Limit free energy on a slice

title: Proof ideas
body_md:
The core of the proof of Theorem~\ref{t.slices} consists of two facts: the enriched free energy of a slice satisfies the Hamilton--Jacobi equation \eqref{e.slice.hj} up to an error term that is small, and the initial condition $\psi_m$ is convex as a function of the path variable, so that the solution has the Hopf representation \eqref{e.slice.hopf}. 

In the usual formulation of the Hamilton--Jacobi approach \cite{chen2024ms, chen2026ising, chen2025free, chen2026spherical, HJbook, mourrat2021nonconvex, mourrat2022parisi, mourrat2023free, mourrat2020extending}, the enriched free energy is defined by coupling the spins to a Gaussian field indexed by a Poisson--Dirichlet cascade, the path $q$ prescribing the covariance between the fields at two leaves of the cascade as a function of their overlap. The Gibbs measure then features a cascade variable in addition to the spin configuration, and the error term in the PDE vanishes if and only if the overlap of two configurations sampled from the Gibbs measure is determined by the overlap of the cascade variables; see for instance \cite[(6.79)]{HJbook}. Showing that the error term is small thus requires the overlap of the configurations to synchronize with the overlap of the cascade variables. This synchronization is derived from the ultrametricity of the Gibbs measure, by the mechanism of \cite{pan.multi, pan.potts, pan.vec}, and ultrametricity itself is only known after a perturbation of the Hamiltonian, using the approach of \cite{pan.aom} based on the Ghirlanda--Guerra identities. What we obtain then is comparable to knowing that a function solves a Hamilton--Jacobi equation only almost everywhere, which does not suffice to identify it in general, and overcoming this difficulty is a major challenge.

In this paper, we use instead an equivalent definition of the enriched free energy that does not resort to any cascade and that features a single random field, which we call the branch. The branch is a stochastic process $X$ on $[0,1]$, taking values in $\mathbb R^N$, and the enriched Hamiltonian features a term $X_1 \cdot \sigma$ in addition to the terms already present in~\eqref{e.def.free.energy}. The law of the branch corresponds, in the setting of the cascade formulation, to the law of the Gaussian field attached to a leaf that is selected according to the Gibbs weights. This law can be described explicitly as the solution of a stochastic differential equation in $\mathbb R^N$; we refer to Section~\ref{s.branch} for the precise definition. Appendix~\ref{s.cascade} is not necessary for the purposes of showing any result in this paper, but we provide it to explain in more detail this correspondence between the classical definition of the enriched free energy and the one we adopt here. 

With this definition, the derivatives of the free energy necessarily take a different form from the classical one. They involve a family of Gibbs measures indexed by the time variable of the branch; this family corresponds to a disintegration of the usual Gibbs measure from the cascade representation according to the value of the overlap between the cascade variables. Controlling the error term in the PDE then amounts to showing that the overlap concentrates under these Gibbs measures. Adapting the approach of~\cite{aronow2026quantitative} for obtaining a quantitative proof of the Parisi formula for the SK model without external field, we show that the fluctuations of the overlap under these Gibbs measures are indeed small, with an explicit bound in terms of $N$ and of a lower bound on the derivative of the path (Theorem~\ref{t.remainder}). One key observation is that conditionally on a sampled configuration, the Gaussian data have a log-concave law, and one can therefore use the Brascamp--Lieb inequality to control the fluctuations of functionals of the disorder. No perturbation of the Hamiltonian is involved. This argument bounds the fluctuations conditionally on the sampled configuration. By working on a slice, we ensure that intra-species permutations of the coordinates act transitively on the model, and thus for observables that are invariant under this transformation, the conditioning can be removed. In the model without external field studied in \cite{aronow2026quantitative}, the spin-flip symmetry is used instead to cover the full configuration space, but the presence of an external field breaks the invariance under such transformations. 

The second role played by the restriction of the free energy to slices concerns the initial condition. The Hopf representation of the solution to a Hamilton--Jacobi equation requires a convex initial condition, and the initial condition $\psi_\circ(\cdot;h)$ of the model with a fixed field $h$ is not convex in the path when $h$ is large, as was pointed out in \cite[Section~6]{mourrat2021nonconvex}. Fixing the magnetization changes this: we prove that~$g_m$ is convex as a function of the path variable. That $\psi_\circ(\cdot;0)=g_0$ satisfies this property has already been shown in \cite{chen2026ising, ho2026concavity}, and here we extend this property to every $m$. This yields a variational representation for the limit free energy over each slice, which we turn into the uninverted formula \eqref{e.slice.martingale} using convex-duality arguments, and the full free energy is finally recovered by minimizing over the slices, as in \eqref{e.full.slices}. 

To close this introduction, we also mention that the existence of the limit free energy of a broader class of spin-glass models was very recently shown in \cite{ho2026convergence}, also using ideas from~\cite{aronow2026quantitative}. Now that the existence of the limit free energy is established for this broader class of models, we can appeal to \cite{chen2024ms, chen2025free} to assert that this limit can be represented in terms of a (possibly non-unique) critical point of an explicit functional. 


\medskip

\noindent \textbf{Organization of the paper.} Sections~\ref{s.branch} to~\ref{s.derivatives} define the enriched free energy and derive the identities for its derivatives, as outlined above, both for the full system and for the one restricted to a slice. This yields that the error term in the Hamilton--Jacobi equation is controlled by an average of the variances of the overlap under the family of Gibbs measures discussed above. Section~\ref{s.concentration} shows that these variances are small on a slice, uniformly over the slices, once the slopes of the path are bounded below, following the method of~\cite{aronow2026quantitative}. Section~\ref{s.scalar} presents several properties of the scalar function~$g_m$, including that it can be represented as an infimum over martingales started at $m$, and that it is a convex function of the path variable. Section~\ref{s.initial} identifies the limit of the initial condition $\overline F_{N,k}(0,\cdot)$ as $\psi_{m_{N,k}}$, uniformly over the slices. Section~\ref{s.hj} uses this to show \eqref{e.slice.convergence}--\eqref{e.slice.hopf} of Theorem~\ref{t.slices}. Section~\ref{s.duality} turns the Hopf formula into the martingale formula via a convex-duality argument, yielding \eqref{e.slice.martingale}. Section~\ref{s.conclusion} shows \eqref{e.full.slices} and completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{t.main}. Finally, Appendix~\ref{s.cascade} relates the enriched free energy used here to its classical definition through Poisson--Dirichlet cascades; the main text does not depend on the results of this appendix.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{l.wellposed}
Let $q$ be regular, and fix a realization of $g$. There is a unique function $U=U(\cdot,\cdot\,;g)$ on $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^N$, continuous and with $|\partial_{x_i}U|\leqslant1$ for every $i$, which is a classical solution of \eqref{e.branch.pde} on each piece of $q$ and satisfies the terminal condition \eqref{e.def.terminal}. Its spatial derivatives of all orders are continuous and bounded on $[0,1]\times\mathbb R^N$, and $\partial_rU$ is bounded and continuous away from the breakpoints of $q$.
head: environment
name: Well-posedness of the branch equation

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by backward induction on the pieces of $q$. On a piece $[s_j,s_{j+1}]$, the matrix $D$ is constant and positive definite, so that \eqref{e.branch.pde} is a uniformly parabolic semilinear equation with coefficients that are smooth in $r$ and a nonlinearity that is quadratic in the gradient. The terminal datum at $s_{j+1}$ is \eqref{e.def.terminal} for the last piece, and otherwise the value already constructed at $s_{j+1}$; in both cases it has bounded derivatives of all orders. The standard theory of such equations, see for instance \cite[Chapter~V]{LSU}, provides a unique classical solution with bounded derivatives of all orders on the piece, the gradient bound below supplying the a priori estimate needed for global existence; the solution converges to its terminal datum in every $C^k$ norm as $r\uparrow s_{j+1}$. Hence the spatial derivatives of the glued function are continuous across $s_{j+1}$. Each partial derivative $w:=\partial_{x_i}U$ solves the linear equation $\partial_rw+\operatorname{tr}(D
abla^2w)+2r\,
abla U\cdot D
abla w=0$, with terminal datum in $[-1,1]$, so the maximum principle gives $|w|\leqslant1$. Uniqueness among continuous solutions with bounded gradient is the case $\phi_1=\phi_2=0$ of Lemma~ef{l.comparison} below.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{l.wellposed}, It\^o's formula applies on each piece of $q$, and gives
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm d U(r,X_r;g)
 &=\bigl(\partial_rU+\operatorname{tr}(D\nabla^2U)+2r\,\nabla U\cdot D\nabla U\bigr)(r,X_r;g)\,\mathrm d r
   +\boldsymbol m_r\cdot\sqrt{2D(r)}\,\mathrm d B_r\\
 &=r\,\boldsymbol m_r\cdot D(r)\boldsymbol m_r\,\mathrm d r+\boldsymbol m_r\cdot\sqrt{2D(r)}\,\mathrm d B_r,
\end{align*}
where we used \eqref{e.branch.pde}. Integration over $[0,1]$ gives \eqref{e.ito.identity}. The stochastic integral has zero mean since $|\boldsymbol m_r|\leqslant\sqrt N$, and \eqref{e.free.energy.unpacked} gives \eqref{e.free.energy.V}.

title: Proof
body_md:
We write $H_N(\sigma)=g\cdot v_\sigma=\sum_ag_ah_a(\sigma)$, where $h_a(\sigma)$ denotes the $a$-th coordinate of $v_\sigma$ in an orthonormal basis of the disorder space, so that $\sum_ah_a(\sigma)h_a(\tau)=N\xi(R_N(\sigma,\tau))$ by \eqref{e.gram}. For a deterministic vector $G$ in the disorder space, let $\Psi(G)$ denote $\mathbb E\,U(0,X_0;g)$ computed with the terminal condition $\log\sum_{\sigma\in\Omega}w(\sigma)e^{G\cdot v_\sigma+x\cdot\sigma}$; then $\mathbb E\,U(0,X_0;g)=\mathbb E\Psi(\sqrt{2t}g)$. Since $\sqrt{2t}g$ is a centered Gaussian vector with covariance~$2t\mathrm{Id}$, and since $\Psi$ is smooth with bounded second derivatives (by the polarized form of \eqref{e.response.zero}, $|\partial_{G_a}\partial_{G_b}\Psi|\leqslant\|h_a\|_\infty\|h_b\|_\infty$), the heat equation gives, for every $t\geqslant0$,
\begin{equation*}
 \partial_t\mathbb E\,U(0,X_0;g)=\mathbb E\sum_a\partial^2_{G_a}\Psi(\sqrt{2t}g)
 =\sum_a\mathbb E\Xi_0(h_a),
\end{equation*}
because a change of $G_a$ perturbs the terminal Hamiltonian by the fixed observable $h_a$, and the second variation of $U(0,X_0;g)$ in that direction is the response \eqref{e.def.response}. By \eqref{e.response.zero} and \eqref{e.gram},
\begin{align*}
 \sum_a\mathbb E\Xi_0(h_a)
 &=\int_0^1\mathbb E\sum_a\operatorname{Var}_u(h_a)\,\mathrm d u\\
 &=\int_0^1\mathbb E\Bigl\langle N\xi\bigl(R_N(\sigma,\sigma)\bigr)
                  -N\xi\bigl(R_N(\sigma^1,\sigma^2)\bigr)\Bigr\rangle_u\,\mathrm d u\\
 &=N\xi(\lambda_N)-N\int_0^1\mathbb E\langle\xi(R_N)\rangle_u\,\mathrm d u ,
\end{align*}
since $R_N(\sigma,\sigma)=\lambda_N$ for every $\sigma\in\Sigma_N$. The self-overlap correction $t\xi(\lambda_N)$ in \eqref{e.free.energy.V} cancels the first term, and the second identity in \eqref{e.derivatives} follows. At $t=0$, the derivative of $t\mapsto\mathbb E\Psi(\sqrt{2t}g)$ is a right derivative, and the right-hand side is continuous in $t$.

title: Proof
body_md: The set of regular paths is convex, so $q+\varepsilon(q'-q)$ is regular for $\varepsilon\in[0,1]$, with the admissible variation $h=q'-q$. By Theorem~\ref{t.derivatives} and $0\leqslant p_{N,s}(r)\leqslant\lambda_{N,s}$, the derivative along this segment is bounded in absolute value by $\sum_s\lambda_{N,s}\|q'_s-q_s\|_{L^1}$, and since $\lambda_{N,s}\geqslant0$ and $\sum_s\lambda_{N,s}=1$, we have $\sum_s\lambda_{N,s}|x_s|\leqslant\max_s|x_s|\leqslant|x|$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^{\mathscr S}$, which gives the second inequality in \eqref{e.finite.lipschitz} after integration in $r$. Since $R_N(\sigma^1,\sigma^2)\in[-1,1]^{\mathscr S}$ and the coefficients of $\xi$ are nonnegative, $|\partial_t\overline F_{N,\Omega}|\leqslant\sup_{[-1,1]^{\mathscr S}}|\xi|=\xi(\mathbf1)$. Regular paths are dense in $\mathcal Q_1^{\mathscr S}$: a path in $\mathcal Q_1^{\mathscr S}$ is approximated in $L^1$ by bounded paths, which are approximated by continuous piecewise affine increasing paths, and adding $\eta(1+r)\mathbf1$ with small $\eta>0$ makes them regular.

title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Convexity in the Gaussian data

title: Proof
body_md: The terminal datum \eqref{e.def.terminal} is smooth in $(x,g)$ with bounded derivatives of all orders, so the regularity follows from Lemma~\ref{l.wellposed} and the smooth dependence on parameters noted after Lemma~\ref{l.comparison}. Fix a direction $(\widehat x,\widehat g)$ with $|\widehat x|^2+|\widehat g|^2=1$. By Lemma~\ref{l.symmetries}(1) and the uniqueness in Lemma~\ref{l.wellposed}, we have $U(r,x+y\widehat x;g+y\widehat g)=U^y(r,x;g)$, where $U^y$ solves the equation with the terminal Hamiltonian perturbed by $y\,b(\sigma)$ with $b(\sigma):=\sqrt{2t}\,\widehat g\cdot v_\sigma+\widehat x\cdot\sigma$. The proof of Lemma~\ref{l.response}, applied to the branch started from $(r,x)$, shows that $\partial_y^2U^y(r,x;g)|_{y=0}$ is a nonnegative combination of conditional variances of $b$, with total weight one, as in \eqref{e.response.second}. This gives the convexity, and the upper bound in \eqref{e.joint.hessian.bound} follows from $b(\sigma)^2\leqslant(|\widehat x|^2+|\widehat g|^2)(|\sigma|^2+2t|v_\sigma|^2)=N(1+2t\xi(\lambda_N))$, by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and \eqref{e.gram}.

In the normalization \eqref{e.parisi.normalization}, with the Brownian motion $W_t:=B_{Tt}/\sqrt T$ on $[0,1]$ and the external field $h=y$, \cite[Lemma~2.2]{mourrat2025uninverting} states that
\begin{equation*}
 \Phi(0,y)=\sup_{\widetilde\alpha}\mathbb E\left[\frac12\int_0^1\xi_T''(t)\mu([0,t])\widetilde\alpha_t^2\,\mathrm d t
 +\widetilde\alpha_1\int_0^1\sqrt{\xi_T''(t)}\,\mathrm d W_t-\phi^*(\widetilde\alpha_1)\right],
\end{equation*}
where the supremum is over the bounded martingales $\widetilde\alpha$ on $[0,1]$ in the completed filtration of $W$, and where $\phi^*(z)=I(z)-yz$ for $z\in[-1,1]$ and $\phi^*(z)=+\infty$ otherwise is the convex conjugate of $x\mapsto\log\cosh(x+y)$; moreover, the supremum is attained exactly at $\widetilde\alpha_t=\partial_x\Phi(Tt,\widetilde X_t)$, where $\mathrm d\widetilde X_t=\xi_T''(t)\mu([0,t])\partial_x\Phi(Tt,\widetilde X_t)\,\mathrm d t+\sqrt{\xi_T''(t)}\,\mathrm d W_t$ and $\widetilde X_0=y$. The map $\alpha\mapsto\widetilde\alpha$, $\widetilde\alpha_t:=\alpha(Tt)$, is a bijection from $\mathcal M_T$ onto the set of bounded martingales $\widetilde\alpha$ with $|\widetilde\alpha_1|\leqslant1$ almost surely, and the other bounded martingales have objective $-\infty$. Substituting $t=v/T$, the objective becomes $\int_0^T\zeta(v)\alpha(v)^2\,\mathrm d v+\sqrt2\,\alpha(T)B(T)-I(\alpha(T))+y\,\alpha(T)$, and $\mathbb E[\alpha(T)]=\alpha(0)$. This gives \eqref{e.scalar.sup.martingale}. Finally, $\widetilde X_t=X^y_{Tt}$, so the maximizer is $\widetilde\alpha_t=M^y_{Tt}$, that is, $\alpha=M^y$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 2: the lower bound.}\par
Let $\alpha\in\mathcal M_T$. By Fubini's theorem, since $\zeta(v)=\nu([0,v])$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.fubini.chi}
 \int_0^T\zeta(v)\mathbb E[\alpha(v)^2]\,\mathrm d v
 =\int\nu(\mathrm d w)\int_w^T\mathbb E[\alpha(v)^2]\,\mathrm d v
 =\chi_\alpha(T)-\int\chi_\alpha\,\mathrm d\nu.
\end{equation}
Since $T-\chi_\alpha(T)=\int_0^T(1-\mathbb E[\alpha(v)^2])\,\mathrm d v$, the objective in \eqref{e.scalar.sup.martingale} is $y\,\alpha(0)+T-c_T(\alpha)-\int\chi_\alpha\,\mathrm d\nu$, and \eqref{e.scalar.sup.martingale} reads
\begin{equation}\label{e.scalar.sup.rewritten}
 \Phi(0,y)=T+\sup_{\alpha\in\mathcal M_T}\Bigl\{y\,\alpha(0)-c_T(\alpha)-\int\chi_\alpha\,\mathrm d\nu\Bigr\}.
\end{equation}
For $\alpha\in\mathcal M_T^m$, this gives $c_T(\alpha)+\int\chi_\alpha\,\mathrm d\nu\geqslant T-\Phi(0,y)+ym=\psi_\circ(\nu;y)+ym$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$, and taking the supremum over $y$ in \eqref{e.def.g.m}, we obtain $c_T(\alpha)+\int\chi_\alpha\,\mathrm d\nu\geqslant g_m(\nu)$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 3: attainment for $|m|<1$.}\par
Let $y:=y(\nu,m)$ and $\alpha:=M^y$, which belongs to $\mathcal M_T^m$ by \eqref{e.def.y.m}. Since $\alpha$ attains the supremum in \eqref{e.scalar.sup.rewritten}, we have $c_T(\alpha)+\int\chi_\alpha\,\mathrm d\nu=T-\Phi(0,y)+ym=g_m(\nu)$, by the choice of $y$ in \eqref{e.def.g.m}.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 4: the endpoints.}\par
Let $m=1$. For the constant martingale $\alpha\equiv1$, we have $c_T(\alpha)=I(1)=\log2$ and $\chi_\alpha(x)=x$, so Step~2 gives $g_1(\nu)\leqslant\log2+\int v\,\nu(\mathrm d v)$. For the reverse inequality, let $y\in\mathbb R$, $X:=X^y$, $M:=M^y$ and $m_y:=M_0$. By \eqref{e.scalar.optimal.value} and the identity $\log\cosh x=x-\log2+\log(1+e^{-2x})$,
\begin{equation*}
 \Phi(0,y)\leqslant\mathbb E[X_T]-\log2+\mathbb E\bigl[\log(1+e^{-2X_T})\bigr]
 -\int_0^T\zeta(v)\mathbb E[M_v^2]\,\mathrm d v.
\end{equation*}
By \eqref{e.scalar.diffusion} and the martingale property, $\mathbb E[X_T]=y+2m_y\int_0^T\zeta$, and $2m_y-\mathbb E[M_v^2]\leqslant2m_y-m_y^2\leqslant1$ by Jensen's inequality, so that
\begin{equation*}
 \Phi(0,y)\leqslant y-\log2+\int_0^T\zeta+\mathbb E\bigl[\log(1+e^{-2X_T})\bigr].
\end{equation*}
Since the drift in \eqref{e.scalar.diffusion} is at least $-2$, we have $X_T\geqslant y-2T+\sqrt2B_T$, so for $y\geqslant2T$ the last integrand is bounded by $\log(1+e^{-2\sqrt2B_T})$, which is integrable, and it tends to zero as $y\to\infty$. By dominated convergence, $\sup_y\{y-\Phi(0,y)\}\geqslant\log2-\int_0^T\zeta$, that is, $g_1(\nu)\geqslant T+\log2-\int_0^T\zeta=\log2+\int v\,\nu(\mathrm d v)$, since $\int_0^T(1-\zeta)=\int v\,\nu(\mathrm d v)$. This proves \eqref{e.g.endpoints} for $m=1$, and shows that the infimum is attained at $\alpha\equiv1$. The case $m=-1$ follows by the symmetry $x\mapsto-x$.

body_md:
\noindent\emph{Step 1: smoothness, and directional derivatives.}\par
Let $|m|<1$ and $0<q_0<\cdots<q_\ell<T$. On the open cone of such heights, $\Phi_{\nu_q}(0,y)$ is a smooth function of $(q_0,\ldots,q_\ell,y)$, as a finite composition of the operators \eqref{e.def.gaussian.operator}, which depend smoothly on their parameter $a$; and $y(\nu_q,m)$ is a smooth function of the heights by the implicit function theorem, since $\partial_x^2\Phi_{\nu_q}>0$. Hence $g_m(q)=T-\Phi_{\nu_q}(0,y(\nu_q,m))+my(\nu_q,m)$ is smooth on this cone.

We now compute directional derivatives. Let $a\in\mathcal Q_\infty$, and let $\gamma$ be a bounded measurable function on $[0,1)$ such that $a_\theta:=a+\theta\gamma$ belongs to $\mathcal Q_\infty$ for all small $\theta>0$, with uniform norms bounded by some $T'$, and let $\nu_\theta:=\nu_{a_\theta}\in\mathcal P([0,T'])$. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{e.directional.derivative}
 \lim_{\theta\downarrow0}\frac{g_m(a_\theta)-g_m(a)}{\theta}
 =\int_0^1\chi'_{\nu_0,m}(a(r))\,\gamma(r)\,\mathrm d r.
\end{equation}
For every potential $\chi$, we have $\int\chi\,\mathrm d(\nu_\theta-\nu_0)=\int_0^1[\chi(a_\theta(r))-\chi(a(r))]\,\mathrm d r$, so the supporting inequality \eqref{e.scalar.support}, applied at $\nu_\theta$ and at $\nu_0$, gives
\begin{equation*}
 \int_0^1\bigl[\chi_{\nu_\theta,m}(a_\theta(r))-\chi_{\nu_\theta,m}(a(r))\bigr]\,\mathrm d r
 \leqslant g_m(a_\theta)-g_m(a)
 \leqslant\int_0^1\bigl[\chi_{\nu_0,m}(a_\theta(r))-\chi_{\nu_0,m}(a(r))\bigr]\,\mathrm d r.
\end{equation*}
Each integrand is $\theta\gamma(r)$ times the average of the derivative of the corresponding potential over the segment between $a(r)$ and $a_\theta(r)$. Since $\int_0^{T'}|\zeta_{\nu_\theta}-\zeta_{\nu_0}|=W_1(\nu_\theta,\nu_0) \leqslant\theta\|\gamma\|_{L^1}$, Corollary~\ref{c.scalar.support} gives $\chi'_{\nu_\theta,m}\to\chi'_{\nu_0,m}$ uniformly as $\theta\downarrow0$, and $\chi'_{\nu_0,m}$ is continuous. Dividing by $\theta$ and letting $\theta\downarrow0$, both bounds converge to the right-hand side of \eqref{e.directional.derivative}, by bounded convergence.

For the finite-step path $q$ with distinct heights and $\gamma=\1_{[r_i,r_{i+1})}$, the paths $a_\theta$ are increasing for small $\theta$, and $\chi'_{\nu_q,m}(q_i)=\mathbb E_m[M_{q_i}^2]$ by Corollary~\ref{c.scalar.support}, so \eqref{e.directional.derivative} proves \eqref{e.scalar.path.derivative}. For general $a\in\mathcal Q_\infty$, the function $v\mapsto\mathbb E[(M^{\nu_a,m}_v)^2]=\chi'_{\nu_a,m}(v)$ is increasing with values in $[m^2,1]$, by the martingale property and Jensen's inequality, and composing it with the increasing path $a$ gives the properties of $z_a$ stated in \eqref{e.def.z.a}. Taking $\gamma=b-a$ with $b\in\mathcal Q_\infty$, for which $a_\theta$ is a convex combination of $a$ and $b$, \eqref{e.directional.derivative} says that $\int_0^1z_a(b-a)$ is the right derivative of $\theta\mapsto g_m(a+\theta(b-a))$ at $\theta=0$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 2: off-diagonal entries of the Hessian.}\par
Let $K_{ij}:=\partial_{q_i}\partial_{q_j}g_m(q)$ and $U_i(q,z):=\mathbb E_z[M_{q_i}^2]$, so that $K_{ij}=w_i\partial_{q_j}U_i(q,m)$ by Step~1. Let $j\ne i$. Increasing $q_j$ lowers $\zeta_{\nu_q}$ on the interval swept by the atom, and leaves the observation time $q_i$ unchanged. By Lemma~\ref{l.diffusion.comparison}(2), the diffusion coefficient $A$ decreases, and then, by Lemma~\ref{l.diffusion.comparison}(3), $\mathbb E_m[\varphi(M_{q_i})]$ decreases for the convex function $\varphi(z)=z^2$. Hence $\partial_{q_j}U_i(q,m)\leqslant0$, that is, $K_{ij}\leqslant0$ for all $j\ne i$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 3: row sums of the Hessian.}\par
Let $0<\varepsilon<T-q_\ell$, and consider the path $q+\varepsilon\mathbf1$, with all heights shifted by $\varepsilon$. We write $\widetilde\Phi$ and $\widetilde A$ for the associated objects, and $\widetilde M$ for its magnetization process started at time $0$ from $m$. The cumulative function of $\nu_{q+\varepsilon\mathbf1}$ is $\zeta_{\nu_q}(\cdot-\varepsilon)$ on $[\varepsilon,T]$, and $\Phi(T-\varepsilon,\cdot)=\log\cosh+\varepsilon$ by \eqref{e.scalar.top}, since $T-\varepsilon>q_\ell$. Since the operators $T_{r,a}$ commute with the addition of constants, the recursion \eqref{e.def.scalar.recursion} gives $\widetilde\Phi(v,x)=\Phi(v-\varepsilon,x)-\varepsilon$ for $v\in[\varepsilon,T]$, so that $\widetilde A(v,z)=A(v-\varepsilon,z)$. By \eqref{e.scalar.diffusion} and \eqref{e.def.magnetization.process}, it follows that for every $z\in(-1,1)$, the processes $(\widetilde M^{\varepsilon,z}_{\varepsilon+r})_{r\in[0,T-\varepsilon]}$ and $(M^{0,z}_r)_{r\in[0,T-\varepsilon]}$ have the same law, where $M^{0,z}$ is the magnetization process for $q$. The $i$-th height of $q+\varepsilon\mathbf1$ is $q_i+\varepsilon$, so by the Markov property, the convexity in the starting point of Lemma~\ref{l.diffusion.comparison}(1), and Jensen's inequality for the martingale $\widetilde M$,
\begin{equation*}
 U_i(q+\varepsilon\mathbf1,m)
   =\mathbb E\bigl[\widetilde M_{q_i+\varepsilon}^2\bigr]
   =\mathbb E\bigl[U_i(q,\widetilde M_\varepsilon)\bigr]
   \geqslant U_i\bigl(q,\mathbb E\widetilde M_\varepsilon\bigr)=U_i(q,m).
\end{equation*}
Differentiating at $\varepsilon=0$ gives $\sum_j\partial_{q_j}U_i(q,m)\geqslant0$, that is, $\sum_jK_{ij}\geqslant0$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 4: conclusion.}\par
For every real vector $\theta=(\theta_0,\ldots,\theta_\ell)$,
\begin{equation*}
 \theta^{\mathsf T}K\theta
 =\sum_i\Bigl(\sum_jK_{ij}\Bigr)\theta_i^2
                +\sum_{i<j}(-K_{ij})(\theta_i-\theta_j)^2\geqslant0,
\end{equation*}
by Steps~2 and~3. This proves that $g_m$ is convex on the open cone of distinct positive heights. The Lipschitz bound \eqref{e.scalar.lipschitz} is the $W_1$ bound of Lemma~\ref{l.legendre.m}, since $W_1(\nu_q,\nu_{q'})=\|q-q'\|_{L^1}$. Convexity extends by continuity to coincident or zero heights, hence to all finite-step paths, any two of which share a common partition, and then by density and \eqref{e.scalar.lipschitz} to $\mathcal Q_1$. For $m=\pm1$, the function $g_m$ is affine by \eqref{e.g.endpoints}.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 5: the supporting inequality.}\par
Let $|m|<1$ and $a,b\in\mathcal Q_\infty$. Since $g_m$ is convex on $\mathcal Q_1$, the function $\theta\mapsto g_m(a+\theta(b-a))$ is convex on $[0,1]$, so it lies above its tangent line at $\theta=0$, which by Step~1 is $\theta\mapsto g_m(a)+\theta\int_0^1z_a(b-a)$. Taking $\theta=1$ gives \eqref{e.scalar.supporting}.

body_md:
We first prove the entropy estimate. Let $\mathsf h(p):=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p)$ for $p\in[0,1]$, with $0\log0=0$. Writing $p=\frac{1+z}2$ in the definition of $I$, we get $I(z)=p\log(2p)+(1-p)\log(2(1-p))=\log2-\mathsf h(\frac{1+z}2)$, and since $\frac{1+m_k}2=\frac kn$, we have
\begin{equation*}
 I_{n,k}-I(m_k)=\mathsf h\bigl(\tfrac kn\bigr)-\frac1n\log\binom nk.
\end{equation*}
Let $p:=k/n$ and $b_j:=\binom nj p^j(1-p)^{n-j}$ for $0\leqslant j\leqslant n$, so that $\sum_jb_j=1$ and $b_k=\binom nk e^{-n\mathsf h(p)}$. In particular, $b_k\leqslant1$. If $k\in\{0,n\}$, then $b_k=1$. Otherwise, for $0\leqslant j<n$, the ratio $b_{j+1}/b_j=\frac{(n-j)k}{(j+1)(n-k)}$ is at least $1$ for $j<k$ and less than $1$ for $j\geqslant k$, since $(n-j)k-(j+1)(n-k)=n(k-1-j)+k$. So $b_k$ is the largest of the $n+1$ numbers $b_j$, and $b_k\geqslant(n+1)^{-1}$. Thus $(n+1)^{-1}e^{n\mathsf h(k/n)}\leqslant\binom nk\leqslant e^{n\mathsf h(k/n)}$, that is, $0\leqslant I_{n,k}-I(m_k)\leqslant\frac{\log(n+1)}n$.

We now turn to the proof of \eqref{e.composition}. By~\eqref{e.finite.lipschitz}, both sides of this inequality are continuous in $a$ for the $L^1$ norm, so it suffices to consider a regular path $a$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 1: uniform weights, and a coupling of the two slices.}\par
Since $2^{-n}=e^{-nI_{n,k}}\binom nk^{-1}$, and since adding a constant to the terminal datum adds it to the solution of the branch equation, by Lemma~\ref{l.symmetries}(1), the quantity $G_{n,k}(a)-I_{n,k}$ is the free energy at $t=0$ of the slice $\Omega_{n,k}$ with the uniform weights $\binom nk^{-1}$. Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be independent random variables, uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$. Let $\sigma\in\Omega_{n,k}$ be the configuration whose plus spins are the $k$ sites with the smallest values of $U_i$, and define $\sigma'\in\Omega_{n,k'}$ in the same way with $k'$. Then $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$ are each uniformly distributed on their slices, and they differ at exactly $d:=|k-k'|$ sites. Let $\widetilde\Omega\subseteq\{-1,1\}^{2n}$ be the set of pairs $(\sigma,\sigma')$ obtained in this way, with the weights $w(\sigma,\sigma')$ given by their probabilities. Since $\sum_{\sigma'}w(\sigma,\sigma')=\binom nk^{-1}$ for every $\sigma\in\Omega_{n,k}$, the slice $\Omega_{n,k}$ with the uniform weights is the projection of $(\widetilde\Omega,w)$ on the first block of $n$ coordinates, in the sense of Lemma~\ref{l.block}, and $\Omega_{n,k'}$ with the uniform weights is its projection on the second block.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 2: a doubled system.}\par
For $u\in[0,1]$, consider the system with $2n$ coordinates, partitioned into two species, the first and the second block of $n$ coordinates, with the configuration set $\widetilde\Omega$ and the weights $w$, at $t=0$, with the path $q^u:=((1-u)a,ua)$. Its free energy, normalized by $2n$ as in Definition~\ref{d.free.energy}, is $\overline F_{2n,\widetilde\Omega}(0,q^u)$, and we set $G(u):=2\overline F_{2n,\widetilde\Omega}(0,q^u)$. The auxiliary field of this system has two blocks, driven by independent Brownian motions, with covariance paths $(1-u)a$ and $ua$; the terminal weights couple the two blocks. Since $\lambda=(\frac12,\frac12)$ for this system, the self-overlap correction $2\lambda\cdot q^u(1)=a(1)$ does not depend on $u$. The function $G$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ by \eqref{e.finite.lipschitz}. At $u=0$, the second path vanishes, and Lemma~\ref{l.block} together with Step~1 gives $2n\overline F_{2n,\widetilde\Omega}(0,(a,0))=n\bigl[G_{n,k}(a)-I_{n,k}\bigr]$, that is, $G(0)=G_{n,k}(a)-I_{n,k}$; similarly, $G(1)=G_{n,k'}(a)-I_{n,k'}$. For $u\in(0,1)$, the path $q^u$ is regular, and $u\mapsto q^u$ is an admissible variation with $h=(-a,a)$, so by Theorem~\ref{t.derivatives}, with the overlaps $\frac1{2n}\sigma^1\cdot\sigma^2$ and $\frac1{2n}\sigma'^1\cdot\sigma'^2$ of the two blocks, the function $G$ is differentiable on $(0,1)$, with
\begin{equation*}
 G'(u)=\frac1n\int_0^1a(r)\,
 \mathbb E\bigl\langle\sigma'^1\cdot\sigma'^2-\sigma^1\cdot\sigma^2\bigr\rangle_r\,\mathrm d r,
\end{equation*}
where $(\sigma^1,\sigma'^1)$ and $(\sigma^2,\sigma'^2)$ are two replicas at level $r$. Since $\sigma^b$ and $\sigma'^b$ differ at $d$ sites, at most $2d$ terms of the sum defining $\sigma'^1\cdot\sigma'^2-\sigma^1\cdot\sigma^2$ are nonzero, each bounded by $2$. Hence $|G'(u)|\leqslant\frac{4d}n\|a\|_{L^1}=2|m_k-m_{k'}|\,\|a\|_{L^1}$ on $(0,1)$, and \eqref{e.composition} follows by the continuity of $G$ on $[0,1]$.

oindent\emph{Step 1: the evolution.}\par
Write $\chi^*_T(p):=\sup_{y\in [0,T]}(p\cdot y-\chi(y))$, which is a finite convex function of $p$, separable in the coordinates. Since $\chi^*_T\leqslant\chi^*$, the right-hand side of \eqref{e.localized.evolution} is at least $\mathsf S_t\chi(x)$. For the converse, let $c_s:=\lambda_s\chi_{s}'(T_s-)$ be the left derivative of $\lambda_s\chi_s$ at $T_s$. If $p_s\geqslant c_s$, the concave function $y_s\mapsto p_sy_s-\lambda_s\chi_s(y_s)$ is increasing on $[0,T_s]$, so its supremum over $[0,T_s]$ is attained at $y_s=T_s$, and $\chi^*_T$ is affine in $p_s$ with slope $T_s$ on this range. There, the derivative in $p_s$ of the objective in \eqref{e.localized.evolution} is $x_s+t\partial_s\xi(p)-T_s\leqslant x_s+t\partial_s\xi(\lambda)-T_s\leqslant0$, because $\partial_s\xi$ is coordinatewise increasing on $\mathbb R_+^{\mathscr S}$. Hence decreasing $p_s$ to $c_s$ does not decrease the objective. After doing this in every coordinate, we obtain a point $p$ with $p_s\leqslant c_s$ for all $s$; for such $p$, the function $y_s\mapsto p_sy_s-\lambda_s\chi_s(y_s)$ is decreasing on $[T_s,\infty)$, so $\chi^*(p)=\chi^*_T(p)$. The right-hand side of \eqref{e.localized.evolution} is therefore at most $\mathsf S_t\chi(x)$. The supremum is attained by continuity and compactness. The last two assertions follow, since $\chi^*_T$ only involves $\chi$ on $[0,T]$, and $\chi\leqslant\chi'+c$ on $[0,T]$ implies $\chi^*_T\geqslant\chi'^*_T-c$.
